body: A phone held at arm’s length above a face is the only light in the room at eleven at night. The twenty-three-year-old lying under it in the dark came off a warehouse shift at nine. He has eaten, he has showered, and he is not doing anything now that he would describe as doing anything. He is halfway down a thread about a man he has never met and will never meet. In eleven minutes he will put the phone face down on the carpet, and in six hours he will be awake again with something sitting in his chest that he cannot name, and he will not connect the two.

What he handed himself was not the thread. It was the state he was in while he read it — mildly agitated, mildly behind, quietly judging somebody. That is what went to the night shift, and the night shift works on whatever it is given.

There is nothing mystical about the last ten minutes before sleep. The mind keeps working on the last thing it was handed, and it does so for several hours without supervision, without your consent, and without anything you can do about it once you are under.

Belong is the word in the title, and it is worth taking literally. Ten minutes is a small enough piece of a day that nobody thinks of it as property, which is exactly why it is the easiest piece to take. Nobody schedules the last ten minutes. They are whatever is left over when the deciding has stopped for the day — and a very great deal of design has gone into making sure that what is left over is a feed. The slot already has an owner. It is simply not you, it never asked, and the arrangement holds every night of the year because you have never once thought of that stretch as a thing that could be given to somebody on purpose.

The dial this article is going to send you to runs from HM 300.30 to HM 398.70 and carries 121 stations, each holding one frequency permanently. Somewhere on it, at eleven o’clock tonight, something is already playing that nobody arranged for you.

Defending that slot costs something, and the cost is that you have to decide in advance, at an hour when you feel perfectly capable of deciding later. Nobody at eleven at night believes they need a rule. The rule is not for the version of you that is fine. It is for the Tuesday in February when a phone call went badly and the flat has gone quiet and you would much rather be distracted than settled. You do not get to choose what you think about at four in the morning. You do get to choose what you handed yourself at eleven.

It is worth saying plainly how strange it has become to end a day on purpose. Nearly every other threshold has kept its form — people still mark a wedding, still stand up at a funeral, still do something particular on a birthday. The end of a day is crossed several hundred times a year and has quietly lost every marker it ever had. There is no reason for that beyond convenience. Something arrived that would fill the gap without being asked, and the practice that used to fill it was never formally abandoned. It was simply outbid, ten minutes at a time.

The old forms understood the mechanism better than we tend to credit. Compline is short, it is fixed, and it says roughly the same thing every night regardless of what the day contained. So does the blessing said over a child at a bedside, which has survived a very long time in houses that agreed on almost nothing else. Neither one asks you to feel anything. Both are built so that a tired person can complete them badly and still get the benefit.
That is the design worth copying. Something outside you, saying the same thing, at the same hour, whether or not you are up to it.

The obvious modern answer is to choose better — a calm playlist, a sleep track, something picked because it suits you. That answer is not stupid, and for a while it works. Its problem is that it puts the decision back at the exact hour when your judgement is worst. Choosing what to listen to means opening the thing that holds everything else as well, and thinking about your own state long enough to select for it, and both of those are the opposite of closing a day. The nights you most need it are the nights you will pick badly, or pick nothing, or find yourself back in the feed with the playlist still unopened.
Something that is already playing has already made the decision.

A woman in her fifties gets in from a late shift at a care home at twenty past ten, and the house is asleep. She eats standing up at the counter. She has done this three nights out of seven for eleven years, and the part she has never got used to is not the work but the hour afterwards, when she is too wired to sleep and too tired to be any use to anybody. For the last few months she has put the small speaker on in the kitchen while she does the plates, and left it going while she goes up, and turned it off from the doorway of her room. She could not tell you one thing it has played. She has stopped lying awake.
Nothing in that was a devotional practice, and she would not call it one. Something else occupied the slot, and it was not hostile, and that turned out to be the entire requirement.

The honest cost is that this does not work as a mood. Some nights the music will be wrong for where you are — too bright when you are flat, too slow when you are still wound up, a language you do not speak arriving at half past eleven. You are not the editor. Somebody scheduled it hours ago and went home, and there will be evenings when you would genuinely rather have chosen.

That is not a fault to be designed out. The reason it works is precisely that it does not consult you, because consulting you is the failure mode. Every night you are asked what you want at eleven is a night the answer can be the feed, and in the bad weeks the answer will be. Something that plays whether or not you approve of it is the only kind of thing still running on the night you are least able to arrange anything at all.

So the claim here is narrow. Ten minutes at the end of a day is the one slot with several unattended hours attached to it. It is currently owned by something that never asked. It can be given, deliberately and without ceremony, to something that will say an ordinary true thing while you brush your teeth. That is the whole of it, and it is worth considerably more than it sounds.
All of which is theory until something is actually playing at eleven o’clock tonight. So here is the part that is not theory.

The dial is not a library and it is not arranged like one. Stations sit in blocks — a five-fold band of ministry stations, a run of frequencies for the nations in their own languages, a mainstream band of always-on formats — and once you know roughly where a block sits you can put a hand on it without looking. 46 frequencies are on air now, across 29 languages, and every one of them is running whether or not anybody is tuned to it. There is no queue to build and no evening playlist to assemble. There is a number, and behind the number something already in progress.

For this particular use, start at HM 314.40 — Midnight Praise. It is the ambient worship frequency, and it exists for the end of a day rather than the middle of one: long, slow, largely instrumental, built to be left running in a room where somebody is winding down rather than paying attention. That last part matters more than it sounds. Most music that calls itself calm is still trying to be interesting, and interesting is the wrong ambition at eleven at night — it keeps the mind sitting up in bed. Midnight Praise is content to be the thing in the background while you put the day away. Put it on in the kitchen, leave it going while you go up, and turn it off from the doorway.

There is nothing to install. No app, no download and no card. Open kJubilee.com on whatever phone is nearest, press play, and it plays — it is built deliberately for inexpensive phones and thin connections, so it starts on the hardware people actually have. If you want it closer to hand, add the page to your home screen and it opens like anything else there. And do make yourself an account while you are at it. It is free, it keeps your favourites with you across every Jubilee site, and it is how the band finds out which frequencies people are reaching for at which hours — which is how the next one gets built, and how this one gets better at eleven o’clock.

So do not evaluate it. Evaluating is a decision, and the whole point of the slot is that it should not require one. Tonight, before you sit down, put HM 314.40 on, and then get on with the ordinary business of ending a day. Give it a week of unremarkable nights. You will not be able to say what it played, and that is not a failure of the station. You will simply find that four in the morning has got quieter, and you will not have had to feel a single thing to get there.
